title: Response patterns for request saturation and latency incidents
content:
Purpose: quick operator reference for common API surface incidents we keep seeing: client-side timeouts, 429s due to request saturation, degraded streaming (chunk loss or stalls), and sudden rise in 5xx/error-rate. Not a full postmortem — ops-first checklist + short investigation patterns and durable remediation notes.

Scope: public API endpoints (text generation, streaming, embeddings), internal edge/proxy layer, and gateway rate-limiter interactions. Assumes familiarity with our observability dashboards, k8s namespace naming, and common tooling (kubectl, curl, jaeger, datadog/metrics, prometheus).

Quick severity guide (for triage):
- Sev2 (user-facing degradation): visible latency > 2x SLO for >5% of traffic OR streaming stalls impacting >= 3 distinct customers.
- Sev1 (partial outage): >50% request failures (5xx/timeout/429) for a route for >5 minutes OR downstream GPU pool fully saturated with request backlog.
- Note: use business-impact first — customer escalations can elevate priority.

Immediate one-liners (first 7 minutes):
- Post to #sre-ops with headline, route(s), approximate % of traffic impacted, and a short next-step (eg: "rolling restart candidate"). Use the incident template snippet in Slack pinned messages.
- Open a lightweight incident ticket (JIRA prefilled template SRE-INC).
- If streaming clients: disable streaming fallback in gateway (route-level flag) to force non-streaming fast-path for affected customers while investigating.

Observability checklist (what to glance at first):
- Global metrics: 1m P90 latency, 5m error-rate, 1m rate of 429s, inflight request count.
- Edge / Gateway: requests/sec per route, token bucket utilisation, rate-limiter dropped tokens (promql: sum(rate(gateway_rate_limiter_drops_total[1m])) by (route)).
- Upstream serving: GPU pool queue depth, host CPU/mem, KV cache hit ratio, batching latency distribution.
- Streaming: gap metric (stream_chunk_gap_seconds), delay between first and last chunk, client ack errors.
- Traces: sample 5 traces from failing requests (jaeger link). Look for: long queue time, repeated retries, blocked RPC to model worker.
- Recent deploys: check merged PRs in last 60 minutes (GitHub) and cluster rollout events.

Quick mitigations (fast, low-risk):
- Apply adaptive throttling: reduce per-customer burst quota for the route in gateway (feature flag).
- Temporarily increase worker replicas or scale GPU pool (if capacity available) — prefer autoscale policy if configured.
- Route fallback: switch route to lower-capacity model variant with same API contract (if verified). Note: partially reduces quality but stabilizes latency.
- Disable expensive hooks: telemetry sampling, synchronous writes to external services (metrics pushback), or third-party integrations causing latency.
- If 429s are gateway-originated due to token bucket exhaustion, apply short-term token refill bump (10–30s) to reduce head-of-line queuing while we investigate.

Commands / snippets (operators):
- Check gateway rate limits (kubectl): kubectl -n gateway exec -it gateway-0 -- curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep rate_limiter_drops
- Inflight requests per backend: kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=model-worker -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | xargs -n1 -I{} kubectl -n serving exec {} -- curl -s localhost:9100/metrics | grep inflight
- Identify long traces (jaeger): query by operation "api.generate" + tag "status=timeout" -> inspect spans for queue/serialization time.
- Quick test to reproduce (non-prod preferred): curl -H "Authorization: Bearer TEST" -d '{"input":"short"}' https://api.staging.redwood.ai/v1/generate?stream=true -v

Degraded streaming specifics (common symptoms / fixes):
Symptoms: client sees initial token(s) then long silence; chunk order replays; 502/stream reset mid-session.
Likely causes: upstream worker OOM/killed, reverse-proxy chunk buffer overflow, network flaps between gateway and worker, aggressive idle timeouts on LB, or kernel-level socket backlog.
Immediate steps:
- Check worker pod logs for OOM/kills: kubectl -n serving logs <pod> --previous | grep -i oom
- Check proxy (envoy/nginx) buffers and timeouts; bump stream_idle_timeout for route to 60s if currently lower.
- If chunk drops correlate with a particular model: scale that model's workers to reduce per-instance load, enable smaller batch sizes.
- If backlog in GPU pool: temporarily route streaming traffic to non-stream batch endpoint with reduced chunk frequency.

Handling 429 storms / request saturation:
- Distinguish source: gateway-issued 429 vs. upstream worker-initiated 429 (we have 2 codes: 429.GW and 429.BACKEND).
- If gateway 429 (token bucket exhaustion): reduce ingress rate via global burst limit for offending route and contact client teams if misbehaving clients found.
- If backend 429 (service-level): look at worker thread pool, blocking RPCs to KMS/HSM, or slow disk. Collect worker-side 429 counters: sum(rate(worker_429_total[1m])) by (instance).
- Backoff heuristics for clients: recommend Exponential backoff with jitter (base 200ms, max 10s). Publish a suggested header X-Backoff-Hint in gateway responses (ops-only quick patch).

Elevated 5xx/error-rate pattern:
- Quick classification: are errors homogeneous (same stacktrace/exception) or heterogeneous?
- If homogeneous: one code path failing — reproduce locally with same input (linked example IDs), find recent PR touching that area.
- If heterogeneous: likely downstream saturation or resource exhaustion. Check open file descriptors, CPU steal, cgroup OOMs.
- Hot fix: rollout a rollback to last known-good image for the service if confidence and approval exist.

Operator scripts and snippets to include in incident ticket:
- Sample curl failure payload and response headers (copy/paste in ticket).
- Prometheus queries used (paste exact queries) so others can reproduce graphs.
- Short trace ids (3) and investigator notes.

Short-term remediation playbook (post-stabilize):
- Run a bounded canary load test on the route to validate throttle settings.
- Add a circuit-breaker rule to protect the GPU pool from bursty traffic.
- Create an alert: high 429 rate with source tag = gateway should page SRE (current alert thresholds tend to be too permissive).

Owner action items (for the next 72h):
- [ ] Correlate root cause with recent deploys and vendor changes.
- [ ] Add regression test for streaming chunk order under simulated packet loss.
- [ ] Review autoscaler thresholds for model worker pools (reduce cooldown, increase upper bound).
- [ ] Draft customer-facing note if any customers saw degraded outputs.

Notes to self / unresolved questions:
- Is X-Backoff-Hint safe to add to prod responses? Need security review re: header leakage.
- We still don't have a robust metric for "first-stream-chunk-latency" on the gateway — add metric.
- Consider per-tenant adaptive batching instead of global batch size; design doc ticket included in linked artifacts.

Post-incident checklist (when incident is closed):
- Write brief timeline with key actions and timestamps in JIRA.
- Add to SRE weekly incident review channel with TL;DR and proposed next steps.
- Track follow-ups in single epic SRE-RESILIENCE-2026.

Appendix: useful queries and header meanings (copyable)
- Gateway drops: sum(rate(gateway_rate_limiter_drops_total[2m])) by (route)
- Inflight queue per worker: avg_over_time(worker_inflight_requests[1m])
- 5xx ratio: increase(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m]) / rate(http_requests_total[1m]))

Slack snippets (short):
- Initial: "Incident: /generate route high 429s. Impact ~30% of requests. Investigating gateway token bucket and GPU queue depth. Paging SRE oncall"
- Mitigation done: "Applied temporary throttling for heavy clients and increased worker replicas; observing drop in 429 rate from 30% -> 4% in 5m."

If you use this doc: please add postmortem summary and outcome. Keep this file as a living one — drop quick notes and small reproductions here, not in the incident ticket body.

-- end --
